d: A blood vessel in the brain becomes blocked or bursts and part of the brain is left without blood. It is an emergency: every minute counts. Types, symptoms, the stroke code, treatments, rehabilitation, prevention and life after stroke.
n: What it is A stroke happens when blood stops reaching part of the brain, because an artery becomes blocked or because it bursts. It is also called a cerebrovascular accident (CVA), cerebral infarction or, in older usage, apoplexy. Neurons have no energy reserves: without oxygen and glucose they begin to die within minutes. In a large untreated stroke, an average of about 1.9 million neurons are lost every minute . Hence the motto "time is brain" . d: Stroke symptoms that go away on their own within minutes. It is not a harmless scare but a warning: the risk of a stroke in the following days is high.
n: What it is A transient ischaemic attack (TIA), sometimes called a "mini-stroke", is a brief episode of neurological symptoms caused by a lack of blood supply to part of the brain, spinal cord or retina, which recovers completely and leaves no lesion on MRI. A clot blocks an artery for a few minutes and then breaks up or moves on. Most last less than an hour , and many less than ten minutes. Up to 24 hours used to be accepted, but MRI showed that many longer episodes did leave a small infarct, and the current definition is based on the absence of a lesion, not on the clock. d: An artery bursts and blood collects inside the brain. The most common cause is high blood pressure. Symptoms, treatment and prevention.
n: What it is An intracerebral haemorrhage (brain haemorrhage) occurs when an artery bursts inside the brain and the blood forms a haematoma that compresses and damages the surrounding tissue. It accounts for 10-15% of strokes , but it is the most serious type: about 40% of patients die within the first month and many survivors are left with lasting effects. There are about 3.4 million cases worldwide each year. Causes Long-standing high blood pressure : the most common cause. It damages the small, deep arteries, which eventually rupture. d: The "worst headache of your life", starting suddenly, may be due to a ruptured brain aneurysm. What an aneurysm is, when it is treated and what to do about a thunderclap headache.
n: What it is A subarachnoid haemorrhage is bleeding into the space around the brain, between the meninges, where cerebrospinal fluid circulates. In about 85% of non-traumatic cases it is due to a ruptured aneurysm . It accounts for about 5% of strokes , but affects younger people (the average age is about 55) and is somewhat more common in women. A brain aneurysm is a small sac-like bulge in the wall of an artery, almost always in the circle of Willis , at the base of the brain. d: Much more than a headache: attacks of throbbing pain with nausea and sensitivity to light that can be disabling for hours or days. Triggers, aura, treating attacks and prevention.
n: What it is Migraine is a neurological disease, not just a headache. It causes repeated attacks of moderate or severe headache lasting 4 to 72 hours , accompanied by nausea and sensitivity to light and noise . It affects about 15% of the population, three times more women than men, and is the second leading cause of years lived with disability in the world, the first in young women. In Spain about five million people have it, according to the Spanish Society of Neurology. It has a strong hereditary component: if one parent has it, the children's risk is much higher. d: The most common headache: a band-like pressure of mild or moderate intensity that does not get worse with movement. Why it happens and how to relieve it without overusing painkillers.
n: What it is Tension-type headache is the most common headache: almost 80% of people have it at some point, and about 3% have it almost daily. It is a pressing pain, like a band or helmet squeezing the head, of mild or moderate intensity, on both sides, which does not get worse with physical activity and does not usually come with nausea. Despite its name, it is not caused only by muscle "tension" or stress, although both play a part. Increased sensitivity of the muscles around the skull and, in chronic forms, altered pain processing in the nervous system are thought to be involved. Types Type F

d: Excruciating pain around one eye, with a watering eye and a blocked nose, that comes in bouts lasting weeks. It is uncommon but has effective treatments, such as oxygen.
n: What it is Cluster headache is one of the most intense pains known. It causes attacks of extreme pain around one eye or in the temple, always on the same side , lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours and recurring one to eight times a day , often at the same time , frequently at night. The attacks come in seasons or "clusters" of weeks or months, separated by months or years without pain. It affects about 1 in 1,000 people, more men than women, and usually starts between the ages of 20 and 40. Symptoms Boring pain, "like a red-hot poker in the eye". d: Electric shocks lasting seconds on one side of the face when talking, eating or brushing your teeth. Why it happens and how it is treated, with medicines or surgery.
n: What it is Trigeminal neuralgia causes electric shocks of excruciating pain in part of the face, lasting from a fraction of a second to two minutes. It is due to irritation of the trigeminal nerve , the fifth cranial nerve , which carries sensation from the face. It mainly affects people over 50 and is somewhat more common in women. It has been called "the suicide disease" because of the intensity of the pain, although today it has effective treatments. d: A tendency of the brain to produce seizures through abnormal electrical discharges of neurons. Types of seizure, causes, tests and treatment. Seven in ten people become seizure-free with medication.
n: What it is Epilepsy is a brain disease that causes repeated seizures without an immediate trigger. A seizure is an excessive, synchronised electrical discharge of a group of neurons, which shows itself in many ways depending on the area of the brain affected. It affects about 50 million people worldwide and about 400,000 in Spain . It can start at any age, although it is more common in childhood and in older people. Having one seizure does not mean having epilepsy : one in ten people will have a seizure in their lifetime, for example from a high fever in childhood, low blood sugar or alcohol.

d: A faint is a brief loss of consciousness because too little blood reaches the brain. It is almost always harmless, but it needs to be told apart from a seizure or a heart problem.
n: What it is Syncope is a brief loss of consciousness caused by a temporary drop in blood flow to the whole brain, with spontaneous and complete recovery within seconds or a few minutes. It is what is commonly called a faint . Almost half of people will have at least one in their lifetime, and it accounts for about 1% of A&E visits. Most are harmless, but some are due to heart disease and warn of a risk of sudden death. That is why every syncope deserves a medical assessment. d: The most common cause of vertigo: seconds of spinning when lying down, turning over in bed or looking up. It is cured in the clinic with a manoeuvre.
n: Dizziness and vertigo are not the same "Dizziness" is a word used for very different sensations: unsteadiness, light-headedness, feeling about to faint, or vertigo. Vertigo is a specific sensation: the illusion that you or your surroundings are spinning or moving . It almost always arises in the inner ear (peripheral vertigo) and, less often, in the brain (central vertigo). See dizziness or vertigo? . What BPPV is Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vertigo: it accounts for one in three cases and affects one in ten people over their lifetime, mostly after 50

d: Lapses in memory or other abilities greater than expected for age, but that do not prevent an independent life. What it means, its causes and why it does not always progress to dementia.
n: What it is Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is an intermediate state between normal ageing and dementia. The person, or those around them, notice that memory or other mental abilities (language, attention, orientation or planning) have got worse than before, and tests confirm it, but they remain independent in daily life. They may need more time or effort, or rely on diaries and reminders, but they manage on their own. It affects 10 to 20% of people over 65, and becomes more common with age. d: The most common cause of dementia. How it begins, how it progresses, how it is diagnosed today with biomarkers, what treatments exist and how to care for someone who has it.
n: What it is Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative disease that gradually destroys neurons and their connections, starting with the areas involved in memory . It is the most common cause of dementia , accounting for 60 to 70% of cases. Around 57 million people live with dementia worldwide, and in Spain about 800,000 have Alzheimer's. Age is the main risk factor: it affects fewer than 2% of people aged 65 and more than 30% of those over 85. d: Cognitive decline caused by strokes or by accumulated damage to the brain's small arteries. It is the second most common cause of dementia and the most preventable.
n: What it is Vascular dementia is the loss of mental abilities caused by damage to the blood vessels of the brain . It is the second most common cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease , accounting for 15 to 20% of cases. Very often both coexist in the same person ( mixed dementia ), especially in older age. Unlike other dementias, it is largely preventable . Causes Small vessel disease : the most common. d: A dementia with fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, Parkinson-like stiffness and restless sleep. Very sensitive to antipsychotics.
n: What it is Dementia with Lewy bodies is the second or third most common neurodegenerative dementia, after Alzheimer's disease . It is caused by the build-up in neurons of the protein alpha-synuclein , which forms clumps called Lewy bodies , the same ones found in Parkinson's disease . For this reason the two are considered part of a single spectrum: if dementia appears before or at the same time as the motor symptoms, it is called dementia with Lewy bodies; if it appears years after Parkinson's, it is called Parkinson's disease dementia. d: A dementia that usually starts before 65 with changes in personality and behaviour or with language problems, rather than forgetfulness.
n: What it is Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a group of neurodegenerative diseases that mainly affect the brain's frontal and temporal lobes , the areas that regulate behaviour , personality , judgement and language . It is one of the most common causes of dementia in people under 65 : it usually starts between 45 and 65, in the middle of working and family life. Memory can be well preserved at first, which delays diagnosis. Clinical forms Behavioural variant The most common. d: The fastest-growing neurodegenerative disease in the world. Tremor, slowness and stiffness, but also non-motor symptoms. Diagnosis, treatment with levodopa and other options, and daily life.
n: What it is Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disease in which the neurons that make dopamine in a small area of the brainstem, the substantia nigra , are gradually lost. Dopamine is essential for the basal ganglia to control movement. It is the fastest-growing neurodegenerative disease in the world: it affects more than 10 million people , and in Spain about 160,000-200,000 . It usually starts around 60, although one in ten patients develop it before 50. It was described in 1817 by the English physician James Parkinson in his "Essay on the Shaking Palsy". d: The most common movement disorder: shaking of the hands when using them, which often runs in families and improves with a little alcohol. It is not Parkinson's.
n: What it is Essential tremor is the most common movement disorder : it affects about 1% of the population and more than 5% of people over 65. It causes an action tremor , which appears when using the hands (writing, drinking from a glass, doing up buttons, eating with a spoon) and disappears at rest, exactly the opposite of the tremor of Parkinson's disease . It can start at any age, with two peaks: in youth and from age 50 onwards. More than half of cases have a family history , with autosomal dominant inheritance, although no single gene has been identified. Symptoms Tremor of both hands and

d: Involuntary muscle contractions that cause abnormal postures or twisting movements, such as spasmodic torticollis or writer's cramp. Botulinum toxin is the standard treatment.
n: What it is Dystonia is a movement disorder in which muscles contract involuntarily and in a sustained way , producing abnormal postures , twisting or repetitive movements, sometimes with tremor. It is the third most common movement disorder, after Parkinson's and essential tremor, although it is underdiagnosed. It is caused by malfunction of the circuits of the basal ganglia , the cerebellum and the cortex that control movement. Types by the area affected Focal : a single part of the body. d: An inherited disease that combines involuntary movements, psychiatric changes and cognitive decline. Each child of an affected person has a 50% chance of inheriting it.
n: What it is Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disease that affects movement , thinking and behaviour . It is caused by a mutation in the HTT gene, which contains an abnormally long repeat of the CAG triplet: 40 or more repeats definitely cause the disease. The abnormal protein, mutant huntingtin, mainly damages the neurons of the striatum (the basal ganglia ) and the cortex. It affects about 5 to 10 people per 100,000 in Europe. Symptoms usually start between 30 and 50 , although there are juvenile (before 20) and late-onset forms. It is named after the American physician G

d: Lack of coordination of movement due to a problem in the cerebellum or its connections. It can be caused by alcohol, a stroke, medicines or inherited diseases such as Friedreich's ataxia.
n: What it is Ataxia means lack of coordination. People with ataxia have difficulty coordinating movements : they walk unsteadily with their legs apart, as if drunk, are clumsy with their hands, speak in a slurred or scanning way (separating the syllables) and may have abnormal eye movements. It is almost always due to a problem in the cerebellum or its connections, although it can also be due to loss of deep sensation (sensory ataxia) or of the inner ear. d: An overwhelming urge to move the legs when resting, especially at night, which prevents sleep. Its link with iron, and treatment.
n: What it is Restless legs syndrome , also called Willis-Ekbom disease , is a neurological disorder that causes an irresistible urge to move the legs , almost always accompanied by unpleasant sensations in them: tingling, burning, "fizzy water in the veins", pulling or pain. It affects 5 to 10% of European adults, although only in 2-3% is it severe enough to need treatment. It is twice as common in women and increases with age. d: An inflammatory disease in which the immune system damages the myelin of the brain and spinal cord. It is the most common cause of non-traumatic neurological disability in young adults. Symptoms, diagnosis and the treatments that have changed its outlook.
n: What it is Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an inflammatory, autoimmune and neurodegenerative disease of the central nervous system. The immune system attacks myelin , the sheath that covers the nerve fibres of the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves, and leaves scars ( plaques or "sclerosis") in multiple places. Axons and neurons are also damaged. It is the most common cause of non-traumatic disability in young adults . It affects about 2.9 million people worldwide and about 55,000 in Spain . d: An autoimmune disease that mainly attacks the optic nerves and the spinal cord, with severe relapses. It differs from multiple sclerosis by an antibody, anti-aquaporin-4.
n: What it is Neuromyelitis optica (NMO), or neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), is a rare and serious autoimmune disease of the central nervous system that mainly attacks the optic nerves and the spinal cord . For a long time it was considered a form of multiple sclerosis , but in 2004 it was discovered that most patients have antibodies against aquaporin-4 (AQP4), a protein found in astrocytes, and it is now known to be a separate disease with different treatment. It affects between 1 and 10 people in every 100,000, far more often women (up to 9 in 10), with an average age at onset

d: A neurodegenerative disease in which the neurons that control the muscles die. It causes progressive weakness affecting the arms, legs, speech, swallowing and breathing. Multidisciplinary care and treatments.
n: What it is Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as motor neurone disease , is a neurodegenerative disease that destroys the motor neurons , which carry movement commands from the brain (upper motor neuron) and from the spinal cord and brainstem (lower motor neuron) to the muscles. Without those commands, the muscles weaken and waste away. What is usually not affected is sensation, sight, hearing, eye control and, in most people, intelligence. About 2 to 3 cases per 100,000 people a year are diagnosed, and in Spain about 4,000 to 4,500 people live with ALS, with around 900 new cases

d: An autoimmune disease in which communication between nerve and muscle fails. It causes weakness that gets worse with effort: a drooping eyelid, double vision, difficulty swallowing.
n: What it is Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system makes antibodies that block communication between nerves and muscles at the neuromuscular junction . The nerve releases acetylcholine, but the muscle's receptors are damaged or blocked, and the muscle responds less and less well. The result is muscle weakness that gets worse with effort and improves with rest . It affects about 15-25 people per 100,000 . It has two peaks: young women (20-40 years) and men over 60, in whom it is increasingly common. Symptoms Drooping eyelids (ptosis), often on one side and varying

d: Paralysis that climbs up from the legs over days, often after an infection. The immune system attacks the peripheral nerves. It requires hospital admission, but most people recover.
n: What it is Guillain-Barré syndrome is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the peripheral nerves , usually days or weeks after an infection . It causes rapidly progressing weakness , over hours or days, which usually starts in the legs and moves upwards. It is the most common cause of acute paralysis in the world since polio was almost eradicated, and affects 1-2 people per 100,000 each year, at any age. It is named after the French neurologists Georges Guillain and Jean-Alexandre Barré, who described it in 1916 in two soldiers in the First World War, together with André St

d: Damage to the nerves that run from the spinal cord to the body. It causes tingling, numbness, burning pain or weakness, often in the feet. Diabetes is the most common cause.
n: What it is Peripheral neuropathy is damage to the peripheral nerves , which connect the brain and spinal cord with the skin, muscles and organs. When many nerves are affected at once it is called polyneuropathy . It is very common: it affects about 2-3% of the population and up to 8% of people over 55. Symptoms The most common form is "stocking and glove" polyneuropathy : it starts at the tips of the toes , slowly rises up the legs and, when it reaches the knees, appears in the hands. d: Tingling and numbness in the first fingers of the hand, especially at night, due to compression of the median nerve at the wrist. The most common entrapment neuropathy.
n: What it is Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common entrapment neuropathy . It happens when the median nerve is compressed as it passes through the carpal tunnel , a narrow channel in the wrist formed by the carpal bones and a fibrous ligament, through which the tendons that bend the fingers also pass. It affects about 3-5% of adults, more often women aged 40 to 60. Symptoms Tingling and numbness in the thumb, index, middle finger and half of the ring finger. The little finger is not affected. d: Half of the face stops moving overnight. The most common form, Bell's palsy, usually recovers. How to tell it apart from a stroke and how to protect the eye.
n: What it is Peripheral facial palsy is weakness or paralysis of one whole half of the face , due to damage to the facial nerve , the seventh cranial nerve . The most common form is Bell's palsy , of unknown cause, which affects about 20-30 people per 100,000 each year . It is named after the Scottish anatomist Charles Bell, who described the nerve in 1821. Symptoms They appear over hours, peaking at 2-3 days: Drooping of one half of the face : the corner of the mouth droops, liquid escapes when drinking, it is hard to whistle or blow. d: Pain that runs down the leg or arm along the path of a compressed nerve root, almost always due to a herniated disc. Most cases improve without surgery within weeks.
n: What it is A radiculopathy is irritation or compression of a nerve root where it leaves the spine. When it affects the lower lumbar roots that form the sciatic nerve (mainly L5 and S1), it causes sciatica : pain that runs from the lower back or buttock down the back or side of the leg, often to the foot. In the neck, cervical radiculopathy causes pain that runs down the arm. Sciatica is very common: about 40% of people will have it at some point, mostly between 30 and 50. d: Genetic diseases in which the muscles gradually weaken and degenerate. The best known is Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which affects boys. New therapies and multidisciplinary care.
n: What they are The muscular dystrophies are a group of more than 30 genetic diseases that cause progressive degeneration of the muscles . They are due to mutations in genes that make proteins needed for the structure and function of muscle fibres. Without them, the fibres are damaged by contraction, die and are replaced by fat and fibrous tissue. It was Guillaume Duchenne who described the best-known form in the 19th century. d: A genetic disease of the motor neurons of the spinal cord that causes weakness from childhood. It has gone from being the leading genetic cause of infant death to having three effective treatments, even more so if given before symptoms.
n: What it is Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a genetic disease in which the motor neurons of the spinal cord are lost, causing progressive weakness and wasting of the muscles, especially those closest to the trunk (hips, shoulders) and the breathing muscles. It affects 1 in every 10,000 newborns and, until recently, was the leading genetic cause of death in childhood . Today it is one of the greatest successes of genetic medicine. d: Inflammation of the meninges, almost always due to an infection. Bacterial meningitis is an emergency that can kill within hours. Symptoms, vaccines and treatment.
n: What it is Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges , the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord, almost always due to an infection . Viral meningitis is the most common and is usually mild. Bacterial meningitis is much less common, but it is an emergency : it can kill within hours, and about one in five survivors are left with after-effects. Each year it causes about 2.5 million cases and more than 200,000 deaths worldwide, according to WHO, which has a plan to defeat it by 2030. d: Inflammation of the brain itself, caused by viruses or by the immune system. Fever with confusion, strange behaviour or seizures means going to A&E. Autoimmune encephalitis was discovered less than twenty years ago.
n: What it is Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain . Unlike meningitis , which inflames the membranes covering it, here the brain tissue itself is affected, so changes in behaviour , consciousness and seizures appear. It affects about 5-10 people per 100,000 each year and is a medical emergency . It has two main groups of causes: infections and autoimmunity , which is now known to be almost as common as infection. d: From a minor knock to a serious injury. What to watch for after a blow to the head, when to go to A&E, how to recover from concussion and when to return to sport.
n: What it is A traumatic brain injury (TBI) is an injury to the brain caused by a blow to the head, a sudden acceleration or deceleration (as in a road traffic accident) or an object that penetrates the skull. It is one of the main causes of death and disability in young people , and increasingly common in older people because of falls . Around 27 million new cases occur worldwide every year. In Spain the estimate is about 200 cases per 100,000 inhabitants a year. d: Damage to the spinal cord that cuts off communication between the brain and the body below the injury. Causes, levels, rehabilitation and research advances.
n: What it is A spinal cord injury is damage to the spinal cord , the cord of nerve tissue that runs inside the spine and connects the brain with the rest of the body. It cuts off communication below the injury, causing paralysis , loss of sensation and disturbances of functions such as bladder, bowel, sexual function, blood pressure or breathing. More than 15 million people worldwide live with a spinal cord injury. In Spain there are about 1,000 new cases a year , and some 50,000 people live with one. d: Abnormal growths inside the skull: some are benign, like meningiomas, and others malignant, like gliomas. Symptoms, diagnosis and treatment.
n: What they are Brain tumours are abnormal growths of cells inside the skull. They can be primary , if they arise in the brain itself or its coverings, or secondary ( metastases ), if they come from a cancer elsewhere in the body. Metastases are in fact the most common brain tumours in adults: they appear in 20-40% of people with cancer, especially of the lung , breast , melanoma and kidney. Primary tumours affect about 25 people per 100,000 each year. They are the most common solid tumour in childhood . d: An excessive build-up of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain's ventricles. In children it makes the head grow; in older people, normal pressure hydrocephalus causes a treatable triad of walking, memory and bladder problems.
n: What it is Hydrocephalus is an excessive build-up of cerebrospinal fluid in the brain's ventricles , the cavities through which this fluid flows. The brain produces about half a litre of cerebrospinal fluid every day, which flows through the ventricles, bathes the brain and spinal cord and is reabsorbed into the blood. If its flow is blocked or it is not reabsorbed properly, the ventricles enlarge and compress the brain tissue. See meninges, ventricles and cerebrospinal fluid . d: A group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by damage to the developing brain, before, during or shortly after birth. It does not get worse over time, and early intervention makes the difference.
n: What it is Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by damage to or a disturbance of the developing brain , before, during or shortly after birth. The damage does not progress , but its effects change as the child grows. It is the most common cause of physical disability in childhood : it affects about 2 in every 1,000 live births, although its frequency has fallen in recent years in high-income countries. In Spain about 120,000 people live with cerebral palsy. It is often accompanied by other problems: epilepsy, intellectual disability, problems with vis

d: A sleep disease with irresistible daytime sleepiness and, in many cases, cataplexy: a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions. It is caused by the loss of hypocretin neurons.
n: What it is Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological sleep disease in which the brain cannot properly regulate the states of wakefulness and sleep . It causes intense daytime sleepiness and the intrusion of fragments of REM sleep (dreaming sleep) into wakefulness. It affects 1 in every 2,000-3,000 people , although it is greatly underdiagnosed: the average diagnostic delay is 8 to 10 years . It usually starts in adolescence or young adulthood. d: Difficulty sleeping at least three nights a week for three months, with tiredness during the day. The most effective treatment is not a pill but cognitive behavioural therapy.
n: What it is Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early , despite having the opportunity to sleep, with consequences during the day : tiredness, irritability, problems with concentration or memory, sleepiness. It is considered chronic when it happens at least three nights a week for three months or more. It is the most common sleep disorder: about a third of adults have symptoms of insomnia at some time, and 10-15% have chronic insomnia. It is more common in women , older people and those with chronic illnesses, pain, anxiety or depression. See sleep . Why it becom

d: Motor and vocal tics that start in childhood and usually improve in adolescence. What tics are, what they are associated with, when to treat them and how behavioural therapy helps.
n: What it is Tourette syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by motor and vocal tics that start in childhood , change over time and last more than a year. Tics are sudden, rapid, repetitive, non-rhythmic movements or sounds. It is named after the French neurologist Georges Gilles de la Tourette , a pupil of Charcot, who described it in 1885. Transient tics are very common: up to one in five children have them at some point. Tourette syndrome affects about 0.5-1% of school-age children, three or four times more often boys. d: A clot blocks one of the veins that drain the brain. It mainly affects young women, starts with a headache and is treated with anticoagulants.
n: What it is Cerebral venous thrombosis is the formation of a clot in the veins or venous sinuses that collect blood from the brain to return it to the heart. d: Most headaches are harmless, like migraine or tension-type headache. These are the warning signs that mean you need urgent medical attention.
n: Most are not serious Headache is one of the most common reasons for seeing a doctor: almost everyone has had one. t: What should I do if someone has a seizure?
d: Stay calm, protect their head, put nothing in their mouth, time it and turn the person on their side when the jerking stops. When to call 112 (or your local emergency number).
n: During a convulsive seizure Most epileptic seizures stop on their own within 1 to 3 minutes . What matters is to keep the person safe until it ends. Remember three words: calm, protect, on their side . Stay calm and stay with the person. Check the time : how long the seizure lasts is the most important information. Move away objects they could hit and, if you can, put something soft under their head (a jacket). Loosen tight clothing around the neck and remove their glasses. Do not hold them down or try to stop the jerking. Do not put anything in their mouth : not your fingers, objects or water

d: Brief tingling from a posture is normal. When it is frequent or persistent, the most common causes are carpal tunnel syndrome, diabetic neuropathy or vitamin B12 deficiency.
n: When it is nothing to worry about Feeling your hand or foot "go to sleep" after leaning on it for a long time, crossing your legs or sleeping on your arm is normal : a nerve is briefly compressed and the feeling goes within minutes once you move.
